script.text: The man behind a detector buried in Antarctic ice just won the Nobel Prize in physics. It catches ghost particles from deep space.

On Tuesday, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences gave the prize to Francis Halzen, an 82 year old Belgian-born physicist at the University of Wisconsin. He wins about 1.2 million dollars for his work on high-energy neutrinos from space.

Neutrinos are tiny, almost massless particles. Trillions pass through your body every second, the Associated Press notes. To catch a few, IceCube watches a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole with more than 5,000 light sensors, waiting for rare flashes.

Those flashes show where the particles come from, opening what the Nobel committee calls a new kind of astronomy. Halzen has worked on the idea since the 1980s. Still, he called the prize a great surprise.

Francis Halzen, an 82-year-old Belgian-born physicist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics for his work on IceCube and high-energy neutrinos from space. IceCube watches a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole for rare flashes of light.
